full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN-VARIANT.** The behaviour is the fragmentation transition of the adaptive (coevolving) voter model. The variant here uses a majority-rule node update, synchronous in effect, with 3 states and rewire-to-same.

**1. Model family.** This is an adaptive-network opinion model. Node states update from their neighbours, and links between discordant nodes are rewired. Rewiring goes to a node of the same state, which is the "rewire-to-same" variant. Here the node update is a local majority rule, not voter-model copying of one random neighbour. There are 3 states, a random sparse graph (mean degree about 4), and N=200.

**2. Specific behaviour: network fragmentation.**
- **Earliest clear sources.**
  - Holme & Newman (2006), "Nonequilibrium phase transition in the coevolution of networks and opinions", Phys Rev E 74, 056108. The abstract describes a continuous phase transition as this parameter is varied, from a regime in which opinions are arbitrarily diverse to one in which most individuals hold the same opinion. This is rewire-to-same with many opinion states. I read the abstract only, not the full text.
  - Vazquez, Eguíluz & San Miguel (2008), PRL 100, 108702. In their model, a link between opposite-state nodes is rewired with probability p, while with probability 1-p one of the nodes takes its neighbor's state. They report that the active and frozen phases correspond to a connected and a fragmented network respectively.
- **Multi-state version.** Vazquez, González-Avella, Eguíluz & San Miguel (2007), PRE 76, 046120. They study the coevolution of network structure and node states in a model of multiple state interacting agents. They find a frozen configuration, composed by disconnected network components whose agents share the same state.
- **Rewire-to-same.** Durrett et al. (2012), PNAS, "Graph fission in an evolving voter model". Their model has an edge broken and one endpoint reconnecting to an individual chosen at random from those with the same opinion. They note that this rewire-to-same model has a phase transition similar to that of Holme and Newman.
- **Majority rule with rewiring.** Carro, Vazquez, Toral & San Miguel (2014), PRE 89, 062802. This is the closest majority-rule source. It uses the majority rule or zero-temperature Glauber dynamics on link states, plus rewiring. It finds that any amount of rewiring is able to drive the network to complete order. The final state is either one component or a network fragmented in two. It also reports a domain of bistability between fragmented and non-fragmented final states at low rewiring rates and finite size.
- **Reviews.**
  - Starnini, "Opinion dynamics: Statistical physics and beyond" (arXiv 2507.11521) mentions coevolving models leading, e.g., to fragmentation–consensus transitions as a function of the rewiring rate.
  - Moment-closure and analytic work on adaptive voter models (arXiv 1211.0449, 1012.1213) also covers the transition.
  - I did not find a single dedicated review of majority-rule adaptive networks.

**3. What differs, and whether it matters.**
- **Majority rule on nodes, with rewire-to-same and 3 states.** I did not find a paper with exactly this combination. The mechanism should carry over, because rewiring removes discordant links and node updates remove disagreement. The fixed point is the same in both: no discordant links, so the network splits into same-state components. Majority rule differs in two ways. It produces local frozen domains (disordered topological traps in Carro et al., which come from majority rule alone), and it has no voter-style noise-driven drift to consensus. So fragmentation is likely easier to reach, and the bistability with one-component outcomes may shift.
- **Probability 1.0 majority update every step, with rewiring at p=0.1 or 0.03 and the update ordering swapped.** Synchronous or every-step majority updating is not what the cited models use. They update one node or link at a time. This is likely to matter for details such as trap formation and oscillation. I would not expect it to change the fact that fragmentation occurs.
- **The unusual fingerprint.** The strong signals are `n_components` of 1.44 and `n_giant` of 0.69. The giant component is large, but there are several others. Type entropy is high (0.65), so more than one type survives. Modularity by type (0.36) and degree CV (0.46) are also elevated. This is consistent with fragmentation into multiple same-type components of unequal size, which is the multi-state fragmented absorbing phase. It also fits a partly fragmented, majority-frozen state. Multi-state models were reported to give several components (Vazquez et al. 2007). I did not find numbers for degree CV or edge turnover in the literature. Rewire-to-same is expected to make degrees heterogeneous, since nodes of a surviving type receive extra links. I did not check this against a source.
- **Short runs.** At 83 programs with low rewiring (p=0.03), the system may not have finished fragmenting. That would explain why the fingerprint differs from textbook examples. It is an inference, not something I verified.

**4. Confidence: medium.** The core phenomenon is well documented, and I read the abstracts of the sources above. I did not find a source for the exact majority-rule, 3-state, rewire-to-same combination. The claim that majority rule shifts the details rests on Carro et al. (links, not nodes) and on my own reasoning.
